headline: Time tracking began with nature's cycles—and transformed how humans coordinate and plan
universal_truth: Time is invisible; we can only measure it by observing things that change
fun_facts: Ancient humans tracked time using moon phases—the word 'month' comes from 'moon'
Before clocks, church bells divided the day—the word 'clock' comes from Latin for 'bell'
Your internal body clock is about 24 hours and 11 minutes—slightly longer than a solar day
discussion_questions: How would your life change without precise timekeeping?
Do you feel time passes at different speeds in different situations?
What natural cycles still influence how you experience time?

hook.title: Welcome
hook.script: Time is invisible. You can't see it, touch it, or directly measure it. Yet humans learned to track it by watching what changes: the sun's position, the moon's phases, the seasons' cycle. We measure time by measuring change.

options.text: I want to learn something new
options.response: Perfect. Curiosity is the first step to understanding. Let's explore this together.
That curiosity is exactly what we need. Let's dive in and discover something amazing.

cliff.title: The Question
cliff.script: Before mechanical clocks, how did people coordinate? How could you agree to meet 'at noon' without a clock to tell you when noon arrived?
cliff.prompt: How did people tell time before clocks?

options.text: They used natural phenomena: sun position, shadows, church bells, and biological rhythms
options.response: Yes. The sun at its highest meant noon. Shadows on sundials tracked hours. Church bells marked prayer times. Nature was the clock.

options.text: Time was approximate—people didn't need precise coordination
options.response: Coordination was looser, but they still tracked time using nature's cues...

q1.title: Moon Months
q1.script: The oldest time tracking followed the moon—about 29.5 days from new moon to new moon. The word 'month' comes from 'moon.' Lunar calendars are still used in many cultures. The sky was humanity's first calendar.
q1.prompt: What's your first impression of "Moon Months"?

options.text: This confirms what I already knew
options.response: Great foundation! Now let's build on that knowledge with something you might not expect...
Perfect starting point! This insight will connect to even more surprising facts ahead.

q2.title: Bell Time
q2.script: Before clocks, church bells divided the day into prayer times. The word 'clock' comes from the Latin 'clocca'—meaning bell. Mechanical clocks were invented partly to ring bells reliably. The bells came first.
q2.prompt: How does this connect to what you already know?

options.response: Exactly. These connections are how knowledge becomes understanding.

options.text: I need to think about this more
options.response: That's a good instinct. Deep understanding takes time. The next fact will help clarify.

q3.title: Your Inner Clock
q3.script: You have a biological clock—your circadian rhythm—that runs about 24 hours and 11 minutes. It syncs to sunlight, regulating sleep, hormones, and alertness. Time lives inside you, not just outside.
q3.prompt: What surprises you most about this?

options.text: I never thought about it this way
options.response: That shift in perspective is exactly the point. New angles reveal new truths.
That's learning in action. When understanding shifts, you're really getting it.

wisdom.title: Today's Wisdom
wisdom.script: Here's today's wisdom: Time is invisible; we measure it through change. Tracking time taught humans to coordinate, plan, and build civilization. The ability to agree on 'when' made complex cooperation possible.
wisdom.prompt: What resonates most with you today?

options.response: That central truth will stay with you. Let it guide your thinking.
Application is where knowledge becomes wisdom. That's the real learning.

outro.title: See You Tomorrow
outro.script: That's Day 109. Tomorrow, we'll discover why clocks exist. Until then, notice how you track time—and how time tracks you.
outro.prompt: Before you go—what will you take from today?

options.response: Reflection deepens learning. Let these ideas simmer in your mind.
Teaching others is the best way to learn. You've already begun the ripple.

growTrack.title: Time Awareness - Notice Your Rhythms
growTrack.learning_objective: Develop awareness of personal time perception
growTrack.activity: Notice how you experience time today. When does it fly? When does it drag? What external cues tell you what time it is—light, hunger, energy levels? You have natural rhythms independent of the clock.
